docs.text: Driver ISF15ACP4 Driver ¶ A C++20 driver for the NKK ISF15ACP4 frameless OLED pushbutton: a 96 x 64 colour display on a write-only SPI bus and a debounced switch, on any MCU. It powers the OLED in the order the datasheet requires, draws, scrolls and reports button presses, long presses and repeats. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that moves bytes on the SPI bus, drives three pins and waits; it does the rest: the power sequence, the controller's initialisation, pixel windows in three colour depths, the drawing engine, scrolling and the switch. OLED pushbutton ISF15ACP4 NKK Switches Display 96 RGB x 64 pixels, passive matrix, 65 536 colours (a 256-colour mode is available) Interface Write-only SPI, mode 0, up to 6.6 MHz, with D/C#, RES# and CS#; there is no MISO Switch SPST normally open, two contacts on the module; debounce, press, release, long press and repeat in the driver Supply VDD 2.4 V to 3.5 V for the logic; VCC for the OLED 14 V to 16 V (ISC15ANP4 and ISC01P: 15 V to 17 V), external, enabled by the driver after the controller is configured Variants ISC15ANP4 (64 x 48) and ISC01P (52 x 36, no switch) as presets What you get ¶ A safe power sequence. The OLED supply is never enabled before the controller has been reset and configured, and the power-down always runs. See Contract . A display and a button, both handled. ISF15ACP4<YourPort> draws pixels, rectangles and lines, scrolls, and Poll() turns the switch into events. See API guide . No readback, and it says so. The bus is write only: the driver cannot know that the controller received a byte. What that means and how it is tested: Limitations . Errors you can act on. Every call returns Result<T> ; an invalid argument sends nothing. Zero-overhead portability. The port is a CRTP class checked by a concept: four required hooks, optional switch, clock and log hooks found at compile time. See Porting . Tested against an independent model of the controller. The model checks the datasheet's power rules and reports a violation when the driver breaks one. See Testing and CI . docs.text: Ambiguities ¶ Where the datasheets leave a value or a meaning open, the choice the driver makes, and the setting that changes it. Each one is a bench step in Limitations until someone runs it. Datasheet sections this page relies on Switch circuit and contact data: NKK Switches ISF15ACP4_FramelessOLED (sheets E4 to E9, no number printed) none printed, Switch specifications (sheet E5), p. 2 Power on and off sequence: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.9 Power ON and OFF Sequence, p. 27 Re-map and data format: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 9.1.6 Set Re-map and Data Format (A0h), p. 37 Drawing engine: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 9.2.1 to 9.2.6 Graphic Acceleration Command Set, p. 48 Variant geometry and column offsets: NKK Switches ISC15ANP4 (sheets E4 to E9, no number printed) none printed, Block diagram and pin configurations (sheet E6), p. 3 Display-only variant: NKK Switches ISC01P (sheets E4 to E9, no number printed) none printed, Switch and OLED specifications (sheets E5, E6), p. 2 Start-up values of each module: NKK Switches OLED application notes none printed (web page), Initialization, Tables 1 to 3, steps 4.1 to 4.18 (Note 1, Note 2), p. 1 Communication, SCK frequency and chip select: NKK Switches OLED application notes none printed (web page), Design Considerations 2 and 5, p. 1 Memory window of each module: NKK Switches OLED application notes none printed (web page), Specifying a Memory Window for Downloading, p. 1 Dim mode, power-down and scrolling rules: NKK Switches OLED application notes none printed (web page), Display Commands Available; Scrolling (Screensaver), Table 4, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The controller is named in the application notes ¶ The NKK sheet (E4 to E6) gives the pin names SS, RES, D/C, SCK and SDI, the 96 RGB x 64 format and the controller block diagram, and does not name the controller. NKK's application notes for the OLED Color SmartDisplay do: "All OLED modules incorporate the same OLED controller (SSD1331)" (Part Numbers), and "The same OLED controller is used for all the three OLED SmartDisplay" (General Information). The driver follows the SSD1331 of Solomon Systech. That the NKK modules have the SSD1331's exact command set, and no changes to it, is still confirmed only by the notes' tables using its opcodes. Setting: none; run the host example's picture on the first module. Colour order ¶ The controller has three colour groups A, B and C, and the RAM word is sent C first. The SSD1331 examples and the NKK note drive A as red and C as blue. Settings: Config::red_on_segment_a says which group carries red on the panel (default true); Remap::reverse_colour_order swaps the segment order (A0h bit 2). The driver combines them so that Color is RGB565 whatever the wiring. If red and blue are swapped on your module, flip red_on_segment_a . Colour depth of the 256-colour mode ¶ The NKK sheet says 256 colours are 8 bits "R 2 bit / G 3 bit / B 3 bit"; the SSD1331 gives 3 bits to C, 3 to B and 2 to A. With A as red these agree. The driver encodes red with 2 bits, green and blue with 3 in this mode. VCC settle time ¶ The sequence in SSD1331 section 7.9 says to wait until VCC is "stable" before the display-on command and gives no time; NKK's application notes say only that VCC "can be enabled any time from this point [RES# released] to before the display is turned ON at the end of initialization" and that it must follow VDD. Still open: nothing settles the wait. Setting: Config::vcc_settle_ms , default 50 ms, valid 1 to 1000 ms (assumed). The right value depends on your charge pump's rise time and load; measure the rail. Drawing engine busy time ¶ Neither the SSD1331 datasheet nor NKK's application notes say how long the drawing engine (line, rectangle, copy, dim, clear) is busy, or what happens to a byte sent meanwhile. The notes mention a "two-byte buffer in the OLED communication" and recommend experimenting with the time between bytes, which is the same open point for the throughput. Still open. Setting: Config::engine_settle_us , default 3000 µs (assumed), valid up to 100 000 µs; the driver waits that long after every engine command. If a bench run shows a drawing command being overwritten, raise it. The model's engine_busy_us makes the same assumption testable. CS# high time and CS# release ¶ Table 21 gives no minimum time CS# must stay high between two transfers, and the NKK notes give none either. The driver's port contract assumes one clock period ( kMinCsHighNs , 150 ns), which every SPI peripheral driver meets by itself between two transfers (assumed). What the notes do settle is the other edge: SS is released only after the transmission has finished (they call releasing it early "a common mistake"), and a command with its data is one session. A port's Write() must return only when the last bit is out, which the contract already says ( Porting ); the driver sends each command, and the three second pre-charge speeds of Table 3 (note 2), in one transfer. Writes while scrolling ¶ The datasheet does not say whether RAM writes during a scroll corrupt the display. The driver refuses them with ScrollActive ; Config::writes_while_scrolling allows them if your bench run shows they are safe. Switch bounce ¶ The NKK sheet gives the contact data (SPST, normally open, 200 mΩ maximum, 100 mA at 12 V) and the notes give no bounce time either (they only say how to wire the switch to a pin with a pull-up). Still open. Setting: ButtonConfig::debounce_ms , default 20 ms (assumed), valid 1 to 1000 ms. Measure the switch with a scope and tighten it; poll at least twice per debounce time. Initialisation values and variant offsets ¶ Settled by NKK's application notes, "Initialization": Table 1 for the ISC15ANP4, Table 2 for the ISC01P and Table 3 for the ISF15ACP4, steps 4.1 to 4.18. Config{} and PresetFor() hold exactly those numbers (contrast, remap, display offset, multiplex ratio, dim settings, power save, phase periods, clock, linear gray scale, pre-charge level, VCOMH, and for the ISF15ACP4 the second pre-charge speeds, steps 4.31 to 4.33), and tests/test_nkk_tables.cpp checks each against the table typed in independently. The column origins 16 and 22 and the widths come from the notes' memory-window commands ("15H 10H 4FH", "15H 16H 49H", "15H 00H 5FH"), and the display offsets 10h and 1Ch from step 4.7; the earlier "centred" derivation gave the same numbers. Where the driver differs from a table, or the notes leave a point open: Steps 4.31 to 4.33 (second pre-charge speed) exist only in Table 3. Tables 1 and 2 do not send them, so the ISC15ANP4 and ISC01P presets set send_precharge_speeds to false and leave the controller at its reset values. Step 4.16 of Table 3 sends BBh 1Dh; Tables 1 and 2 send 12h. Bit 0 of BBh is a reserved zero in the SSD1331 table (9.1.19), so the driver keeps a level (A[5:1], 14 for 1Dh, 9 for 12h) and a flag precharge_bit0 that reproduces NKK's byte exactly; the ISF15ACP4 preset sends 1Dh. Whether the controller ignores bit 0 is not known; the bytes are NKK's own. Step 4.5 (A0h) is 68h for the ISF15ACP4 and 70h for the others, as the presets send. The notes list the A0h option bits and call 10b and 11b in A[7:6] reserved; the SSD1331 gives 10b as 65k colour format 2, and the driver still offers it ( ColorDepth::Colors65kFormat2 ) with that difference noted here: prefer Colors65k . Step 4.11 (ADh 8Eh, master configuration) and step 4.12 (B0h 0Bh, power save off) are what the driver sends. ACh (dim): "The values cannot exceed the maximum level for each color of initialization as noted in steps 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3". Validate() and SetDimSettings() refuse a dim contrast above the start-up contrast of the same colour, and SetContrast() refuses a contrast below the dim contrast; SetDimSettings() also keeps the dim contrast at or below the contrast in force, and a failed ApplyConfig() leaves the limit where it was, so that a restart stays valid. Note 1 on steps 4.1 to 4.3, 4.7, 4.9, 4.11, 4.13 to 4.17: "Changing the set-up values may cause damage to the OLED modules." Nothing in the driver stops you from changing them; the field docs say so. Scrolling (notes, "Scrolling (Screensaver)"): 27h "can only be transmitted during initialization or when the display is off, and scrolling is deactivated"; the driver refuses it only while scrolling is on, so call SetupScroll() before DisplayOn() or after DisplayOff() . The notes' prose also says byte A (columns) "should not be set to 00H or it will deactivate the scrolling for the rest of the session" and that scrolling cannot be reactivated; Table 4 of the same notes and the SSD1331 say 0 means no horizontal scroll. The driver allows columns 0 with a vertical step (a vertical-only scroll); this is not verified on a module. The notes confirm that vertical scrolling needs 64 MUX, which the driver enforces, and that RAM must be rewritten after 2Eh. Master current (87h) "should be used while the display is off (after command AEH)". The driver allows it at any time; the start-up sends it with the display off. The notes' clock limit: the pin list gives a 6.66 MHz maximum SCK and Design Considerations 5 a 6.6 MHz throughput; NKK's kit runs 8 MHz and customers report 16 MHz. The driver keeps kMaxClockHz at the datasheet's 6.6 MHz. Setting: every field is in Config and PresetFor() , and Validate() checks the ranges against the SSD1331. A panel that is dim, tinted or offset by a few columns points here. Hardware check: Limitations . Reset pulse width ¶ The RES# low pulse is at least 3 µs (Table 18) and the reset completes within 2 µs; the driver holds the pulse for DelayUs(3) and waits DelayUs(2) after it. A port whose DelayUs() rounds up to a tick holds it longer, which is allowed. Both are datasheet values, not settings.

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is built: three layers, one of them yours, and what happens in each when you show something. Datasheet sections this page relies on Supply voltages, current and the three power states: NKK Switches ISF15ACP4_FramelessOLED (sheets E4 to E9, no number printed) none printed, Recommended operating conditions (sheets E5, E7), p. 2 Serial interface framing, D/C# and chip select: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.1.3 Serial Interface, p. 17 GDDRAM and colour depth: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.5 Graphic Display Data RAM; Table 9, p. 20 Power on and off sequence: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.9 Power ON and OFF Sequence, p. 27 Command table and parameter counts: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 8 Command Table, Table 10, p. 28 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Drawn from: inc/isf15acp4.hpp public calls ; inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . Layers ¶ Layer Files Owns Core inc/isf15acp4.hpp , src/isf15acp4.ipp The power sequence, configuration, pixel windows, the drawing engine, scrolling, the switch, errors Chip definitions inc/isf15acp4_registers.hpp , inc/isf15acp4_types.hpp , inc/isf15acp4_button.hpp , inc/isf15acp4_detail.hpp The command table and its constants, Config , Error , colours, the debouncer, compile-time helpers Port contract inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp The bus requirements, CtrlPin , DataKind , the SpiPort concept Platform port Your class Bus and pin bring-up, one write-only transfer, two control pins, a delay, optionally the switch pin, a clock, logging The debouncer is a separate class with no port and no clock: ButtonDebouncer::Update(down, now_ms) is a pure state machine, tested alone, and Poll() feeds it from the port. Show something ¶ sequenceDiagram participant App participant Core participant Port App->>Core: EnsureInitialized() Core->>Port: GpioSet(VccEnable, INACTIVE) Core->>Port: GpioSet(Reset, ACTIVE) then INACTIVE Core->>Port: Write(Command, display off, configuration) Core->>Port: Write(Data, 12 288 zero bytes in chunks) App->>Core: DisplayOn() Core->>Port: GpioSet(VccEnable, ACTIVE) Core->>Port: DelayUs(vcc_settle), Write(Command, AFh), DelayUs(100 ms) App->>Core: DrawRectangle(...) Core->>Port: Write(Command, 26h, 22h and 10 parameters) Core->>Port: DelayUs(engine_settle) Every method is one or a few transfers. The core keeps command and pixel buffers as members ( command_ , data_ ), so no call allocates and a Write() always gets a pointer that stays valid until it returns. The controller model in the tests ¶ The tests do not use a register map of the controller. They use a model that behaves like the controller on the pins: it decodes commands from its own copy of Table 10, keeps the display RAM, runs the drawing engine and the scroll state, tracks RES#, VCC, CS# and D/C#, keeps a virtual clock that DelayUs() advances, and records a violation when a rule of the datasheet is broken. Testing and CI describes it. Optional hooks ¶ ReadSwitch() , NowMs() and Log() are found at compile time with named concepts in isf15acp4::detail ; a hook declared with the wrong signature is a static_assert that names it, so a typo is never a silently missing hook. A port without them still gets the full display driver; Poll() returns Unsupported . Design decisions ¶ No canvas, no font. The driver stops at the controller: pixel windows, the controller's own engine and scrolling. A frame buffer would cost 12 kB of RAM that most users of a one-button display do not want to spend, and a font is a data and licence decision for the application. The colour type and WriteWindow() are what a graphics layer needs; see Limitations . A shadow, not a state machine of the chip. Because nothing can be read back, the driver keeps only what it needs to refuse unsafe sequences (initialised, supply on, locked, scrolling). It does not predict what the chip shows. Three colour depths, one API. Color is always RGB565; the driver encodes each pixel for the depth in the configuration, including the segment order that follows from the panel wiring.

They use a model that behaves like the controller on the pins: it decodes commands from its own copy of Table 10, keeps the display RAM, runs the drawing engine and the scroll state, tracks RES#, VCC, CS# and D/C#, keeps a virtual clock that DelayUs() advances, and records a violation when a rule of the datasheet is broken. docs.text: No canvas, no font. The driver stops at the controller: pixel windows, the controller's own engine and scrolling. A frame buffer would cost 12 kB of RAM that most users of a one-button display do not want to spend, and a font is a data and licence decision for the application. The colour type and WriteWindow() are what a graphics layer needs; see Limitations . A shadow, not a state machine of the chip. Because nothing can be read back, the driver keeps only what it needs to refuse unsafe sequences (initialised, supply on, locked, scrolling). It does not predict what the chip shows. Three colour depths, one API. Color is always RGB565; the driver encodes each pixel for the depth in the configuration, including the segment order that follows from the panel wiring.

docs.text: Contract ¶ What the ISF15ACP4 driver promises, what it needs, and the rules a caller follows. The driver inherits the Kokeb Labs driver contract ; this page states only what is specific to it. A change to anything here is a breaking change, listed under Breaking in the changelog . Datasheet sections this page relies on Supply voltages, current and the three power states: NKK Switches ISF15ACP4_FramelessOLED (sheets E4 to E9, no number printed) none printed, Recommended operating conditions (sheets E5, E7), p. 2 Reset circuit and reset pulse: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.4 Reset Circuit; 12 AC Characteristics, Table 18, p. 19 Power on and off sequence: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.9 Power ON and OFF Sequence, p. 27 Dim mode, master configuration and display on and off: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 9.1.11 to 9.1.13, p. 45 Command lock: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 9.1.22 Set Command Lock (FDh), p. 47 Supplies, VCC order and the charge pump: NKK Switches OLED application notes none printed (web page), Pin-outs; Design Considerations 1, Power Requirements VCC (16V); Part Numbers, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Promises ¶ The constructor is noexcept , stores the configuration, does no I/O and cannot fail. EnsureInitialized() is the only way to start the driver. Its first call checks the stored configuration ( InvalidArgument , nothing sent), brings the bus up, drives the supply enable off, resets the controller, sends the whole configuration and clears the display RAM. On any failure the driver stays uninitialised, the supply is off, and the next call starts again from the beginning; once it has succeeded, later calls return Ok with no I/O. Every call that touches the controller returns Error::NotInitialized before EnsureInitialized() succeeds. ApplyConfig() before the start only stores the configuration. The switch works before the start: Poll() reads the pin and needs no controller. InvalidArgument means nothing was sent : no transfer and no pin change. Validate() and each call's own checks run before the first byte. Every port failure propagates as Error::Bus ; no call reports success for a transfer or a pin write that failed. Every wait is a bounded delay on the port's DelayUs() ; nothing waits on a flag the bus cannot read. Config{} holds the module's initialisation values; Validate() the documented ranges. A missing required hook, or a hook with the wrong signature, is a compile error that names it; the optional ReadSwitch() , NowMs() and Log() hooks are found at compile time, and the calls that need them return Unsupported without them. Power order ¶ These rules protect the OLED, which can be damaged by its drive supply being on while the controller is not configured. They are the reason for most of the design, and each has a test against the controller model that fails when the driver breaks it. The OLED supply is never enabled before the controller has been reset and configured. EnsureInitialized() drives the enable off, resets, configures and clears the RAM; only DisplayOn() and DisplayDim() enable it, and only when the driver is initialised. A failed start leaves the supply off. From an unknown state (a fresh object after a warm reset of the MCU) the driver cannot know that the panel is lit: its first act is to drive the enable off, which removes VCC without the display-off command and the vcc_off_ms wait of section 7.9. And if that first pin write fails the supply may still be on: EnsureInitialized() then returns Bus . The power-down always runs. Deinitialize() and DisplayOff() are never refused: not before the start, not while the controller is command-locked or scrolling, not after a failed transfer. They send the unlock and the display-off command in one transfer and drive the supply enable off whether or not that transfer succeeded. Deinitialize() then waits vcc_off_ms (tOFF) because the logic supply may be cut next; DisplayOff() does not wait, the logic supply stays on. A pin that will not switch is reported as Bus and the driver keeps IsSupplyEnabled() true, so the caller is told rather than assured. The display is off before the supply is. The normal order is display off, then supply off. If the display-off transfer fails, the supply is still driven off: the supply is the hazard, so its switch-off never waits on a transfer that failed. The failure is reported, and the controller model flags the unsequenced switch-off as a violation the tests allow only after an injected failure. A failure while turning on switches the supply off again. DisplayOn() that cannot send the display-on command drives the supply off before it returns Bus . VDD is cut only after Deinitialize() returns. docs.text: The constructor is noexcept , stores the configuration, does no I/O and cannot fail. EnsureInitialized() is the only way to start the driver. Its first call checks the stored configuration ( InvalidArgument , nothing sent), brings the bus up, drives the supply enable off, resets the controller, sends the whole configuration and clears the display RAM. On any failure the driver stays uninitialised, the supply is off, and the next call starts again from the beginning; once it has succeeded, later calls return Ok with no I/O. Every call that touches the controller returns Error::NotInitialized before EnsureInitialized() succeeds. ApplyConfig() before the start only stores the configuration. The switch works before the start: Poll() reads the pin and needs no controller. InvalidArgument means nothing was sent : no transfer and no pin change. Validate() and each call's own checks run before the first byte. Every port failure propagates as Error::Bus ; no call reports success for a transfer or a pin write that failed. Every wait is a bounded delay on the port's DelayUs() ; nothing waits on a flag the bus cannot read. Config{} holds the module's initialisation values; Validate() the documented ranges. A missing required hook, or a hook with the wrong signature, is a compile error that names it; the optional ReadSwitch() , NowMs() and Log() hooks are found at compile time, and the calls that need them return Unsupported without them.

docs.text: These rules protect the OLED, which can be damaged by its drive supply being on while the controller is not configured. They are the reason for most of the design, and each has a test against the controller model that fails when the driver breaks it. The OLED supply is never enabled before the controller has been reset and configured. EnsureInitialized() drives the enable off, resets, configures and clears the RAM; only DisplayOn() and DisplayDim() enable it, and only when the driver is initialised. A failed start leaves the supply off. From an unknown state (a fresh object after a warm reset of the MCU) the driver cannot know that the panel is lit: its first act is to drive the enable off, which removes VCC without the display-off command and the vcc_off_ms wait of section 7.9. And if that first pin write fails the supply may still be on: EnsureInitialized() then returns Bus . The power-down always runs. Deinitialize() and DisplayOff() are never refused: not before the start, not while the controller is command-locked or scrolling, not after a failed transfer. They send the unlock and the display-off command in one transfer and drive the supply enable off whether or not that transfer succeeded. Deinitialize() then waits vcc_off_ms (tOFF) because the logic supply may be cut next; DisplayOff() does not wait, the logic supply stays on. A pin that will not switch is reported as Bus and the driver keeps IsSupplyEnabled() true, so the caller is told rather than assured. The display is off before the supply is. The normal order is display off, then supply off. If the display-off transfer fails, the supply is still driven off: the supply is the hazard, so its switch-off never waits on a transfer that failed. The failure is reported, and the controller model flags the unsequenced switch-off as a violation the tests allow only after an injected failure. A failure while turning on switches the supply off again. DisplayOn() that cannot send the display-on command drives the supply off before it returns Bus . VDD is cut only after Deinitialize() returns. The driver waits the datasheet's tOFF; cutting the logic supply sooner leaves the OLED supply on without the controller, which the driver cannot prevent from outside.

docs.text: Examples ¶ One folder per platform under examples/ , each with its own port, built by CI on every pull request. The driver itself has no platform code; Platforms lists what exists. CS# is low for the bytes of one transfer. SCK idles low in mode 0. Power order ¶ State (NKK sheet E7) VDD VCC Controller Driver call 0 off off off before EnsureInitialized() , after Deinitialize() 1 on off reset, configured, RAM cleared, display off EnsureInitialized() , DisplayOff() 2 on on display on DisplayOn() , DisplayDim() The datasheet's sequence (SSD1331 section 7.9) is: VDD on; RES# low for at least 3 µs, then high; VCC on at least 3 µs after RES# falls and after the initialisation commands; display on, 100 ms until the outputs are on. Power-down is display off, VCC off, and VDD off after tOFF (100 ms typical). The driver does the rest of the sequence and leaves VDD to you: cut it only after Deinitialize() has returned. The NKK application notes agree and add three rules. VCC is disabled at power-up (Design Considerations 1 and Initialization); RES# is low for at least 3 µs and VCC may be enabled "any time from this point to before the display is turned ON at the end of initialization" (Initialization), so the driver's order (VCC after the configuration, display on after vcc_settle_ms ) is inside what the notes allow, and the model's rule that the whole configuration precedes VCC is stricter than the notes. VCC can never be below VDD, because of the internal ESD diode from VDD to VCC: when VCC is disabled it is either at VDD or floating. And VCC must not be present after VDD is gone: make the VCC capacitance smaller than the VDD capacitance or add a pull-down on VCC, because the user can cut the power at any time without the turn-off procedure (Design Considerations 1, FAQ "Does the power up/down sequence have to be followed?"). Timing ¶ Parameter Value Driver RES# low pulse 3 µs minimum reg::kResetPulseMinUs Reset complete 2 µs maximum reg::kResetCompleteMaxUs RES# low to VCC on 3 µs minimum reg::kResetToVccMinUs VCC enabled to display on "stable" (SSD1331); the NKK notes give no number either Config::vcc_settle_ms (default 50 ms, assumed ) Display on to outputs on 100 ms reg::kDisplayOnDelayMs Display off to VDD off 100 ms typical Config::vcc_off_ms Drawing command busy time not given in the SSD1331 datasheet or the NKK notes Config::engine_settle_us (default 3 ms, assumed ) Switch bounce not given in the NKK sheets or notes ButtonConfig::debounce_ms (default 20 ms, assumed ) Every row marked assumed is a setting with a reason in Ambiguities , and a bench step in Limitations . Power ¶ Item (ISF15ACP4) VDD 2.8 V, VCC 15 V Source Drive current, all pixels on 11.0 mA typical, 13.2 mA maximum NKK sheet E5 Logic current, all pixels on 0.17 mA typical NKK sheet E5 Sleep, either supply 10 µA maximum NKK sheet E5 The supplies differ by variant (NKK sheets E5, E9 and E11; absolute maximum 19 V VCC and 4.0 V VDD on all three): Variant VDD VCC minimum / typical / maximum Drive current VCC, all pixels on (typical / maximum) Isf15acp4 2.4 V to 3.5 V 14 V / 15 V / 16 V 11.0 mA / 13.2 mA Isc15anp4 2.4 V to 3.5 V 15 V / 16 V / 17 V 3.8 mA / 4.6 mA Isc01p 2.4 V to 3.5 V 15 V / 16 V / 17 V 2.4 mA / 2.9 mA NKK's application notes (pin list, "VCC: Supply voltage for the OLED (15V to 17V)"; Design Considerations 1, "VCC (16V)") state one range for the whole family, 15 V to 17 V with a 16 V charge pump, and the VDD range 2.4 V to 3.5 V. The ISF15ACP4 sheet (E5) is narrower, 14 V to 16 V with 15 V typical, and NKK's charge-pump manual (Revision C, section 1) lists the ISF15ACP4 only with the 15 V IS-CHPMPHP, and the other two with either pump. The driver's tables keep the narrower per-part sheet range for the ISF15ACP4 (the part's own sheet is the safe side: 17 V is above its maximum), and the notes' 15 V to 17 V for the other two. 16 V is inside the range of all three and inside the notes' range; 15 V to 16 V is the common range. Set your regulator to the variant's own range. NKK sells two charge pumps for this (notes, Part Numbers; the pump manual's own figures differ from the notes', so both are given): the IS-CHPMP, 16 V, 21 mA in the notes and 20 mA in the manual, and the IS-CHPMPHP, 100 mA in the notes, 15 V and 130 mA in the manual. Each has a shut-down input: logic high is normal operation, low shuts it down and leaves the output floating (manual, section 3; kit manual: enable high). The IS-CHPMPHP has a pull-down on that input; the IS-CHPMP has none , so a port driving VccEnable for it needs an external pull-down or the supply is undefined while the MCU pin floats. The ISF15ACP4 draws 11 mA typical and 13.2 mA at most (its sheet), which is why the manual lists only the IS-CHPMPHP for it. The module's inputs must not exceed VDD + 0.3 V (NKK sheet E5, absolute maximum): a 3.3 V MCU on a module run at the typical 2.8 V violates it, so run the module and the MCU from the same rail (within 3.5 V) or level-shift. DisplayOff() and Deinitialize() give the sleep state. Config::master_current (0 to 15) scales the segment current: lower it for less heat and a longer life. Variants ¶ Variant Pixels Switch RAM column of the first pixel Isf15acp4 96 x 64 yes 0 Isc15anp4 64 x 48 yes 16 Isc01p 52 x 36 no 22 PresetFor(variant) returns the module's configuration. The pixel counts are on the NKK sheets. The column origins, the display offsets, the multiplex ratios and every initialisation value are the ones in NKK's application notes: Table 1 (ISC15ANP4), Table 2 (ISC01P) and Table 3 (ISF15ACP4), steps 4.1 to 4.18, and the memory-window commands of "Specifying a Memory Window" (columns 10h to 4Fh and 16h to 49h for the two smaller modules, 00h to 5Fh for the ISF15ACP4). tests/test_nkk_tables.cpp checks each number against the table. NKK Note 1: changing the set-up values (contrast, display offset, multiplex ratio, master configuration, phase periods, clock, linear gray scale, pre-charge level, VCOMH) may damage the OLED module. The setters exist for the datasheet's ranges, not for these values; change them only on a module you can afford to lose ( Ambiguities ). The Isc01p has 8 pins , not 10, and no switch contacts. Its order differs from the table above (NKK sheet E11): Pin 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Name VDD SS RES D/C SCK SDI VCC GND The Isc15anp4 has the same 10 pins as the ISF15ACP4. Do not wire an ISC01P from the 10-pin table: its pin 3 is RES and its pin 7 is VCC . docs.text: State (NKK sheet E7) VDD VCC Controller Driver call 0 off off off before EnsureInitialized() , after Deinitialize() 1 on off reset, configured, RAM cleared, display off EnsureInitialized() , DisplayOff() 2 on on display on DisplayOn() , DisplayDim() The datasheet's sequence (SSD1331 section 7.9) is: VDD on; RES# low for at least 3 µs, then high; VCC on at least 3 µs after RES# falls and after the initialisation commands; display on, 100 ms until the outputs are on. Power-down is display off, VCC off, and VDD off after tOFF (100 ms typical). The driver does the rest of the sequence and leaves VDD to you: cut it only after Deinitialize() has returned. The NKK application notes agree and add three rules. VCC is disabled at power-up (Design Considerations 1 and Initialization); RES# is low for at least 3 µs and VCC may be enabled "any time from this point to before the display is turned ON at the end of initialization" (Initialization), so the driver's order (VCC after the configuration, display on after vcc_settle_ms ) is inside what the notes allow, and the model's rule that the whole configuration precedes VCC is stricter than the notes. VCC can never be below VDD, because of the internal ESD diode from VDD to VCC: when VCC is disabled it is either at VDD or floating. And VCC must not be present after VDD is gone: make the VCC capacitance smaller than the VDD capacitance or add a pull-down on VCC, because the user can cut the power at any time without the turn-off procedure (Design Considerations 1, FAQ "Does the power up/down sequence have to be followed?").

The ISF15ACP4 sheet (E5) is narrower, 14 V to 16 V with 15 V typical, and NKK's charge-pump manual (Revision C, section 1) lists the ISF15ACP4 only with the 15 V IS-CHPMPHP, and the other two with either pump. Set your regulator to the variant's own range. NKK sells two charge pumps for this (notes, Part Numbers; the pump manual's own figures differ from the notes', so both are given): the IS-CHPMP, 16 V, 21 mA in the notes and 20 mA in the manual, and the IS-CHPMPHP, 100 mA in the notes, 15 V and 130 mA in the manual. Each has a shut-down input: logic high is normal operation, low shuts it down and leaves the output floating (manual, section 3; kit manual: enable high). The IS-CHPMPHP has a pull-down on that input; the IS-CHPMP has none , so a port driving VccEnable for it needs an external pull-down or the supply is undefined while the MCU pin floats. The ISF15ACP4 draws 11 mA typical and 13.2 mA at most (its sheet), which is why the manual lists only the IS-CHPMPHP for it. The module's inputs must not exceed VDD + 0.3 V (NKK sheet E5, absolute maximum): a 3.3 V MCU on a module run at the typical 2.8 V violates it, so run the module and the MCU from the same rail (within 3.5 V) or level-shift. DisplayOff() and Deinitialize() give the sleep state. Config::master_current (0 to 15) scales the segment current: lower it for less heat and a longer life.

docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake project on any MCU or on your PC, or to an ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++20 library with no dependencies, and one root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler: GCC 10+, Clang 13+ or a current MSVC. The driver uses concepts and requires . CMake 3.16 or later: it generates the version header the driver includes ( isf15acp4_version.h ). No RTOS, heap, exceptions or RTTI: every call is noexcept and returns a Result . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to the version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-isf15acp4.git external/driver-isf15acp4 git submodule update --init external/driver-isf15acp4 Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ , _config/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples are not; the ESP32 example even has its own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ). CMake (any MCU, any host) ¶ This is the MCU-neutral path: the same two lines work for a host build, STM32 (CubeMX CMake projects), RP2040 (Pico SDK), nRF (nRF Connect SDK) or any other CMake toolchain. Platforms lists what has a port today. add_subdirectory ( external/driver-isf15acp4 ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE isf15acp4::isf15acp4 ) isf15acp4::isf15acp4 is an alias of the isf15acp4 INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories (the headers and the generated version header) and requires C++20, so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect ISF15ACP4_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on every target that links the driver ISF15ACP4_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host tests in tests/ and the host example ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-isf15acp4 -B build-isf15acp4 cmake --install build-isf15acp4 --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( isf15acp4 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE isf15acp4::isf15acp4 ) The target is isf15acp4::isf15acp4 in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . The headers and the generated isf15acp4_version.h go to include/isf15acp4/inc/ , the template implementation to include/isf15acp4/src/isf15acp4.ipp . The host CI installs the package and builds a consumer against it on every pull request ( Testing and CI ). ESP-IDF ¶ Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-isf15acp4) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-isf15acp4 (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-isf15acp4.git components/isf15acp4 isf15acp4 (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml isf15acp4 (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : isf15acp4 : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-isf15acp4.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES isf15acp4 (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). The ESP32 example uses the first way, with EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS pointing at the repository root, and works out the folder name in main/CMakeLists.txt ; CI builds it on every pull request. The repository has no idf_component.yml . The component manager does not need one for a git dependency; the manifest is only required to publish to the ESP Component Registry, which these releases do not use. If registry publishing is chosen, the manifest is added at the root then. How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/isf15acp4_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, sources, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target, alias, install rules and the package export, or the ESP-IDF component Tool configuration _config/ Doxyfile, the docs site, Kconfig, clang-format, clang-tidy and the linters Version ¶ The version is set once in the settings file and written into isf15acp4_version.h in the build tree at configure time. The Doxyfile ( _config/Doxyfile ) carries a copy; a host test fails when it differs. Read it at run time: const char * v = isf15acp4 :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0" Next ¶ Quickstart runs the driver on your PC, then on your MCU; Porting writes the port for your MCU.

docs.text: Limitations ¶ What the driver does not do, and what a user should know before relying on it. Datasheet sections this page relies on Serial interface framing, D/C# and chip select: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.1.3 Serial Interface, p. 17 Power on and off sequence: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.9 Power ON and OFF Sequence, p. 27 Charge pump shut-down input: NKK Switches IS-CHPMP and IS-CHPMPHP Manual C, 3. Pin Configurations, p. 5 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The bus is write only ¶ The serial interface has no read path (SSD1331 section 7.1.3; the module has no MISO pin). Consequences: No readback and no verification. Write() returning true means the bytes were clocked out. The driver cannot confirm that the controller saw them, that it is configured, or what is on the screen. A reset or brown-out of the controller is invisible. If VDD dips or a glitch resets the controller, the driver still believes the panel is on and every call still returns Ok . A dark or white panel is the symptom. The recovery is Reinitialize() (power-down, start-up, display on). An application that must be sure the panel shows its picture calls it after a known disturbance (a supply dip, a hot-plug) or on a slow timer, and redraws. The model's brown-out test shows exactly this behaviour. State is the driver's shadow. GetConfig() , GetOutput() , IsScrolling() and IsLocked() report what the driver sent. After a failed transfer, or after TraceCommand() , IsShadowInDoubt() is true until the next Reinitialize() . Verification is by model. The tests check the driver against an independent model of the controller's pins and commands, not against the chip. A mistake the model shares with the driver is not caught: that is why the model is written from the datasheet and not from the driver, and why a bench run is still needed. Not verified on hardware ¶ Nobody has run this driver on a module. Bench steps, in order: Wire the module as in Hardware , with the supply enable pulled down (the IS-CHPMP charge pump has no pull-down of its own). Run the host example's calls on the board: a rectangle and a diagonal. Expect them; a dark panel means the OLED rail, D/C#, RES# or SS#. Compare red and blue pixels; set red_on_segment_a if swapped. Scope VCC against EnsureInitialized() / DisplayOn() : VCC must stay off until DisplayOn() . Measure the VCC rise time and set vcc_settle_ms above it. Draw 20 lines back to back; if one is wrong, raise engine_settle_us . Scope the switch and set debounce_ms . Run each variant's preset on its own module. The values are NKK's (application notes, Tables 1 to 3) and nobody has tried them here. Two points of those notes are open on hardware: BBh bit 0 (Table 3 sends 1Dh, the SSD1331 calls the bit reserved) and a vertical-only scroll (the notes' prose says a zero column byte stops scrolling for the session). Run Deinitialize() with a scope on VCC and VDD: VCC off first, 100 ms, then you may cut VDD. The ESP-IDF example is compiled by CI and not run. This repository's own checks ran on a host only: no GCC, no Cortex-M cross-build, no CodeQL, no clang-tidy. No canvas and no font ¶ The driver has no frame buffer, no text and no bitmap layer. It would be cheap to add a monochrome font, and the decision is to leave it out: a frame buffer is 12 kB of RAM, and a font is the application's data and licence. What is there is what a graphics layer needs: Color (RGB565), MakeColor() , WriteWindow() , WriteWindowRaw() and the controller's own engine. A graphics library can render into a window and hand it to WriteWindow() . Blocking calls ¶ Every call blocks for its bus time and waits: DisplayOn() about 150 ms, Deinitialize() 100 ms, EnsureInitialized() a few milliseconds plus about 12 kB of RAM clearing (about 20 ms at 6 MHz). There is no DMA or asynchronous interface; a port may use DMA inside Write() as long as it returns when the bytes are out. Other ¶ One driver object per module, one task at a time ( Contract ). The 15 V supply and VDD are yours: the driver switches only the enable, and cannot tell whether the rail came up. The switch is read from a GPIO, not from the controller; it needs the ReadSwitch() and NowMs() hooks. The display's contrast, current and clock follow the module's initialisation values, not the datasheet's reset values: see Ambiguities .

After a failed transfer, or after TraceCommand() , IsShadowInDoubt() is true until the next Reinitialize() . Verification is by model. The tests check the driver against an independent model of the controller's pins and commands, not against the chip. A mistake the model shares with the driver is not caught: that is why the model is written from the datasheet and not from the driver, and why a bench run is still needed.

docs.text: Nobody has run this driver on a module. Bench steps, in order: Wire the module as in Hardware , with the supply enable pulled down (the IS-CHPMP charge pump has no pull-down of its own). Run the host example's calls on the board: a rectangle and a diagonal. Expect them; a dark panel means the OLED rail, D/C#, RES# or SS#. Compare red and blue pixels; set red_on_segment_a if swapped. Scope VCC against EnsureInitialized() / DisplayOn() : VCC must stay off until DisplayOn() . Measure the VCC rise time and set vcc_settle_ms above it. Draw 20 lines back to back; if one is wrong, raise engine_settle_us . Scope the switch and set debounce_ms . Run each variant's preset on its own module. The values are NKK's (application notes, Tables 1 to 3) and nobody has tried them here. Two points of those notes are open on hardware: BBh bit 0 (Table 3 sends 1Dh, the SSD1331 calls the bit reserved) and a vertical-only scroll (the notes' prose says a zero column byte stops scrolling for the session). Run Deinitialize() with a scope on VCC and VDD: VCC off first, 100 ms, then you may cut VDD. The ESP-IDF example is compiled by CI and not run. This repository's own checks ran on a host only: no GCC, no Cortex-M cross-build, no CodeQL, no clang-tidy.

docs.text: The driver has no frame buffer, no text and no bitmap layer. It would be cheap to add a monochrome font, and the decision is to leave it out: a frame buffer is 12 kB of RAM, and a font is the application's data and licence. What is there is what a graphics layer needs: Color (RGB565), MakeColor() , WriteWindow() , WriteWindowRaw() and the controller's own engine. A graphics library can render into a window and hand it to WriteWindow() .

docs.text: Every call blocks for its bus time and waits: DisplayOn() about 150 ms, Deinitialize() 100 ms, EnsureInitialized() a few milliseconds plus about 12 kB of RAM clearing (about 20 ms at 6 MHz). There is no DMA or asynchronous interface; a port may use DMA inside Write() as long as it returns when the bytes are out.

docs.text: Mechanization policy ¶ Where each defect class of the catalogue is caught, and how a class moves to a cheaper catch. The goal: a defect is found by the cheapest check that can find it, and reviewers spend their time on judgement, not on what a script can do. Decision rule ¶ Catch a class at the first level that can decide it without judgement, in order of cost: Lint ( tools/preflight.sh , runs in seconds, on every builder's machine). Use it when the defect is a pattern in text or syntax: a forbidden include, a MISRA rule CodeQL reports, a missing else , a parameter name, a symbol named in docs that does not exist, a missing gitlink. Test, model or mutation (host tests, the chip model's fault knobs, fuzz properties, compile-fail cases, mutants of a fix). Use it when the defect is behaviour: what the driver sends or returns when the chip or the bus misbehaves. A test is the right level when the model can be made to misbehave in exactly that way. Independent review question (a reviewer who did not write the code). Use it only for what needs judgement: whether the datasheet was read correctly, whether a state machine is complete, whether the model is independent of the driver, whether a doc claim is true. Every catalogue entry names its level under DETECTION. A class with no lint or test is a review class and costs reviewer time every round; it is a candidate for promotion. Promotion ¶ A defect that reached a reviewer or the CI of a second driver is promoted one level up: review to test, test to lint where a pattern exists. The reviewer who finds the second occurrence writes the promotion item in the round's report; the template maintainer (the agent or person that owns the template branch) implements it before the next driver's first push, or records why it cannot be mechanised in the catalogue entry. A defect that reached a third driver after its promotion means the check is wrong: fix the check first, then look at the driver. Demotion never happens by silence: a check is removed only with a catalogue note saying what replaced it. What a lint may and may not do ¶ It reports file:line , the catalogue id, and the fix. It exits non-zero on a finding, in the preflight and the gate. It has no false-positive tolerance : before merging, it runs over every finished driver and the template; any finding on a driver that CI shows clean is a false positive, and the lint is not merged until it has none (narrow the pattern; do not add an ignore list per driver). It may be conservative the other way (miss cases): then the catalogue says partial and names the review question that covers the rest. It never edits files, never skips silently (a missing tool is reported as a skipped step in the final line, and the gate treats a skipped MISRA or ESP32 step as a failure), and has a selftest with one bad and one good case. It does not replace the CI scan: CI is the final word for MISRA. Recording a new finding ¶ Append the finding to its catalogue entry (driver, review round or CI report file, finding id) and update the count and the index table; add a new entry only when no class fits. Write the check at the level the rules above give: the lint, or the test pattern (model knob, mutant, fuzz property), or the reviewer's question in the skill. Run it over the finished drivers (lint) or add the regression test that fails without the fix (test). Add a CHANGELOG.md entry under [Unreleased] and the template change is released as a new template commit; drivers take it with scaffold.py --check-drift --fix (the skills and tools are managed files), which updates the template pin in .kokeb/template.yml . Mention the catalogue id in the commit subject. The pre-push gate ¶ A driver is cleared for its first push only by kokeb-tools/gate.sh <chip> (the orchestrator's script, one run per driver through the shared Docker lock). It writes a log and a verdict, and PASS needs all of: container preflight ( tools/preflight.sh --container ) with 0 failure(s) and 0 gate failure(s) , including the MISRA scan and the ESP32 builds; a skipped MISRA or ESP32 step is a FAIL; handbook_check reports 0 errors (this includes the library-subset include scan); tools/check_standalone.py passes; template drift: scaffold.py --check-drift reports nothing; no .pdf file is tracked; the examples/esp32/scripts gitlink (mode 160000) is present; the tree is staged as it will be committed. No silent skips: every step prints a line, and a missing tool fails the gate. Roles ¶ Builders write code, models, tests and docs and run host tests and the quick preflight. They do not run the container gate, push, or create repositories. The gate runner is one serialized worker that runs gate.sh for one driver at a time and reports the verdict and the log; it does not edit the driver. Reviewers are read-only and independent. They are given the code, the model, the datasheet, the catalogue and the previous round's report, and never the builder's conclusions (the build report is read only in the claims-vs-code step). They run the review-round protocol. Fixers change the driver, fix at the cause, add the test that fails without the fix, and answer each finding id. The template maintainer applies promotions and keeps the catalogue current. Backlog of promotions (state of the catalogue) ¶ The classes whose target level is above their present level are listed in the catalogue index: RD-12 to RD-18 and RD-23 (MISRA patterns, one misra_lint with a rule per id), RD-20 and RD-22 (ESP-IDF and compile-fail lints), RD-08 ( claims-symbols ), RD-07 (model standalone lint), RD-06, RD-01, RD-02, RD-03, RD-05, RD-10 and RD-25 (shared model knobs and a template mutation runner), RD-21 (host start-up test of the ESP32 port).

docs.text: Porting ¶ Write the port for your MCU's SDK: a class with a few small methods that moves bytes and drives pins. Datasheet sections this page relies on Serial interface framing, D/C# and chip select: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 7.1.3 Serial Interface, p. 17 Serial interface timing: Solomon Systech (copy from the Adafruit mirror) SSD1331 1.2, 12 AC Characteristics, Table 21, p. 57 Communication, SCK frequency and chip select: NKK Switches OLED application notes none printed (web page), Design Considerations 2 and 5, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The driver never calls your SDK. It calls hooks on a class you derive from isf15acp4::SpiInterface<Self> (in inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp ). The base uses CRTP and declares no hook itself; the driver template is constrained by the isf15acp4::SpiPort concept, so calls are resolved at compile time (no virtual functions, nothing to allocate) and a missing or misdeclared hook is a compile error at the point of use. What you implement ¶ Method Required Contract bool EnsureInitialized() noexcept yes Bring the bus and the pins up, each at its idle level, on the first call; true at once afterwards. false makes the driver's EnsureInitialized() return Bus bool Write(DataKind, const uint8_t* data, std::size_t len) noexcept yes One write-only transfer of 1 to 96 bytes (33 for a command; a bus limited to fewer bytes, such as ESP-IDF's SPI without DMA at 64, needs DMA or its own splitting): D/C# low for Command , high for Data , CS# low for all bytes, CS# high at the end. false on any bus error bool GpioSet(CtrlPin, GpioSignal) noexcept yes Drive RES# or the supply enable; false if the pin write failed void DelayUs(uint32_t us) noexcept yes Wait at least us microseconds bool ReadSwitch(bool& high) noexcept no The switch pin's physical level; false on a read failure uint32_t NowMs() noexcept no A free-running millisecond counter, may wrap void Log(LogLevel, const char* message) noexcept no Print one line; message is plain text, never a format string There is no read hook: the bus is write only. The port ¶ my_port.hpp class MyPort : public isf15acp4 :: SpiInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus and the pins up once, each at its idle level (supply off, RES# high, CS# high); // later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_vcc ( false ) && platform_res ( true ) && platform_spi_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One write-only transfer, CS low for all `len` bytes. There is no read. bool Write ( isf15acp4 :: DataKind kind , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_dc ( kind == isf15acp4 :: DataKind :: Data ) && platform_spi_write ( data , len ); } // RES# is active low and the supply enable active high; the port maps the logical level. bool GpioSet ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin , isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const bool active = ( signal == isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal :: ACTIVE ); if ( pin == isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Reset ) { return platform_res ( ! active ); } return platform_vcc ( active ); } // Wait at least `us` microseconds: the reset and the supply waits depend on it. void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Rules the transfer must follow: One call, one transfer. Keep CS# low for all len bytes. A command and its parameters are one transfer: the controller takes the parameters as the bytes that follow the opcode while D/C# stays low, and splitting them is not allowed. D/C# before CS#. Set D/C# for the kind first; it must be stable before the first clock (tAS 40 ns) and held after the last (tAH 40 ns). The bus requirements below : mode 0 (mode 3 also works), MSB first, up to kMaxClockHz . Start at 1 MHz on jumper wires. Raw bytes only. Do not interpret, retry or reorder bytes. Return false for a bus error. The driver turns it into Error::Bus and never ignores it. Return true only when the bytes were clocked out: it does not mean the controller received them, and the driver does not claim that. Bounded time-outs. A stuck bus fails the call; it does not block forever. Bus requirements ¶ The driver states what the controller needs from the bus as constexpr values in inc/isf15acp4_spi_interface.hpp (handbook KB-CPP-123). Check your port's settings against them with static_assert , as both example ports do, so a port that clocks too fast or in the wrong mode does not compile: Constant Value Meaning (SSD1331 section 7.1.3, Table 21) kSpiMode 0 CPOL 0, CPHA 0; mode 3 also works kMsbFirst true Most significant bit first kMaxClockHz 6'600'000 SCK cycle 150 ns minimum kMinCsHighNs 150 CS# high between two transfers: assumed, the table gives none kCsSetupNs , kCsHoldNs 75 , 60 CS# low to the first SCK edge, last SCK edge to CS# high kDcSetupNs , kDcHoldNs 40 , 40 D/C# valid before and after the byte kContinuousWord false Idle SCK time between the bytes of one transfer is allowed kWriteOnly true There is no MISO Control pins ¶ Each control pin has a defined idle level, and the port drives it there before it enables the pin's output and before the driver's first transfer (handbook KB-HW-018). Configuring a pin as an output first and setting its level afterwards gives the module a pulse it did not ask for: a reset, or worse, the 15 V supply on. CtrlPin Module pin Polarity Idle ( INACTIVE ) level Before the first transfer Reset 5 RES active low high Set high, then enable the output VccEnable enable of the 15 V supply active high low (supply off) Set low, then enable the output GpioSignal::ACTIVE always means "function asserted"; the port maps it to the electrical level (RES# ACTIVE is low, the enable ACTIVE is the supply on, inverted for a low-side or P-channel switch). The supply enable must also be off while the MCU resets and boots: use a pull-down on the regulator's enable, because the port's code does not run then. D/C# is set inside Write() . The bytes passed to Write() live in the driver object ( command_ , data_ ). A port that uses DMA must be given a driver object in memory the DMA engine can read (internal RAM on an ESP32, not flash or PSRAM): declare it static or on the heap with DMA-capable capabilities, not in a section the engine cannot reach. Optional hooks ¶ The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with named concepts in isf15acp4::detail . A missing hook falls back in a documented, safe way; a misdeclared one is a static_assert that names it; neither skips a step silently. Hook Used for Without it ReadSwitch() Poll() , ReadSwitchRaw() Those calls return Unsupported ; the display works NowMs() Poll() timestamps and idle timers, NotifyActivity() Poll() and NotifyActivity() return Unsupported Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged A port with every hook: class FullPort : public isf15acp4 :: SpiInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_gpio_write ( kVccGpio , false ) && platform_gpio_write ( kResGpio , true ) && platform_spi_init (); } bool Write ( isf15acp4 :: DataKind kind , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_gpio_write ( kDcGpio , kind == isf15acp4 :: DataKind :: Data ) && platform_spi_write ( data , len ); } bool GpioSet ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin , isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const bool active = ( signal == isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal :: ACTIVE ); return ( pin == isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Reset ) ? platform_gpio_write ( kResGpio , ! active ) : platform_gpio_write ( kVccGpio , active ); } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // Optional: the switch pin's physical level. The driver applies the polarity. bool ReadSwitch ( bool & high ) noexcept { high = platform_gpio_read ( kSwitchGpio ); return true ; } // Optional: a free-running millisecond counter; it may wrap. uint32_t NowMs () noexcept { return platform_millis (); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( isf15acp4 :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level > isf15acp4 :: LogLevel :: Warning ) { return ; } platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } private : static constexpr int kDcGpio = 3 ; static constexpr int kVccGpio = 4 ; static constexpr int kSwitchGpio = 5 ; static constexpr int kResGpio = 11 ; }; isf15acp4 :: Error RecoverFromDarkPanel ( isf15acp4 :: ISF15ACP4 < FullPort >& panel ) { // The bus is write only: a brown-out of the logic supply cannot be detected, only repaired. This // runs the power-down, the start-up and the display-on again. return panel . Reinitialize (). error ; } A GpioSet() that returns void is a compile error: the driver must see a failed pin write, because it drives the supply with it. The compile-fail tests check that rule and the signatures of every hook. Reference implementations ¶ Every port lives with its example, in examples/<platform>/ ; the driver has none. Platforms lists them and how to add one. examples/host/host_isf15acp4_port.hpp : any PC, against a simulated controller. Start from it for a host build or a test bench. examples/esp32/main/esp32_isf15acp4_port.hpp : ESP-IDF, with every hook. Compiled by CI, not run on hardware. Check your port ¶ Build it: the ports on this page are compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over them. Scope the supply enable: it must stay low through EnsureInitialized() and rise only in DisplayOn() . Draw a rectangle and a diagonal ( Quickstart ). A dark panel with no error means a wire, the 15 V rail or the supply enable: the bus gives no other answer. Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each driver object one owner task, or guard every call with one mutex. When several devices share a bus, the port must also serialise the bus. See Contract . Editor setup ¶ The clang-format and clang-tidy configuration is in _config/ , and the repository root has no copy of it. Tools that take a path use it directly; CI does the same: Tool Setting Command line clang-format --style=file:_config/.clang-format , clang-tidy --config-file=_config/.clang-tidy -p build VS Code (C/C++ extension) "C_Cpp.clang_format_style": "file:${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-format" and "C_Cpp.codeAnalysis.clangTidy.args": ["--config-file=${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-tidy"] clangd (VS Code clangd, Neovim, Emacs), CLion These find .clang-format and .clang-tidy only by name, from the file upwards: copy both to the root once ( cp _config/.clang-format _config/.clang-tidy . ). .gitignore lists the copies, so they never reach a commit; copy again after _config/ changes Configure with -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON (clangd: --compile-commands-dir=build ) so the editor sees the same flags as the build.

docs.text: my_port.hpp class MyPort : public isf15acp4 :: SpiInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus and the pins up once, each at its idle level (supply off, RES# high, CS# high); // later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_vcc ( false ) && platform_res ( true ) && platform_spi_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One write-only transfer, CS low for all `len` bytes. There is no read. bool Write ( isf15acp4 :: DataKind kind , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_dc ( kind == isf15acp4 :: DataKind :: Data ) && platform_spi_write ( data , len ); } // RES# is active low and the supply enable active high; the port maps the logical level. bool GpioSet ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin , isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const bool active = ( signal == isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal :: ACTIVE ); if ( pin == isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Reset ) { return platform_res ( ! active ); } return platform_vcc ( active ); } // Wait at least `us` microseconds: the reset and the supply waits depend on it. void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Rules the transfer must follow: One call, one transfer. Keep CS# low for all len bytes. A command and its parameters are one transfer: the controller takes the parameters as the bytes that follow the opcode while D/C# stays low, and splitting them is not allowed. D/C# before CS#. Set D/C# for the kind first; it must be stable before the first clock (tAS 40 ns) and held after the last (tAH 40 ns). The bus requirements below : mode 0 (mode 3 also works), MSB first, up to kMaxClockHz . Start at 1 MHz on jumper wires. Raw bytes only. Do not interpret, retry or reorder bytes. Return false for a bus error. The driver turns it into Error::Bus and never ignores it. Return true only when the bytes were clocked out: it does not mean the controller received them, and the driver does not claim that. Bounded time-outs. A stuck bus fails the call; it does not block forever.

docs.text: Each control pin has a defined idle level, and the port drives it there before it enables the pin's output and before the driver's first transfer (handbook KB-HW-018). Configuring a pin as an output first and setting its level afterwards gives the module a pulse it did not ask for: a reset, or worse, the 15 V supply on. CtrlPin Module pin Polarity Idle ( INACTIVE ) level Before the first transfer Reset 5 RES active low high Set high, then enable the output VccEnable enable of the 15 V supply active high low (supply off) Set low, then enable the output GpioSignal::ACTIVE always means "function asserted"; the port maps it to the electrical level (RES# ACTIVE is low, the enable ACTIVE is the supply on, inverted for a low-side or P-channel switch). The supply enable must also be off while the MCU resets and boots: use a pull-down on the regulator's enable, because the port's code does not run then. D/C# is set inside Write() . The bytes passed to Write() live in the driver object ( command_ , data_ ). A port that uses DMA must be given a driver object in memory the DMA engine can read (internal RAM on an ESP32, not flash or PSRAM): declare it static or on the heap with DMA-capable capabilities, not in a section the engine cannot reach.

docs.text: The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with named concepts in isf15acp4::detail . A missing hook falls back in a documented, safe way; a misdeclared one is a static_assert that names it; neither skips a step silently. Hook Used for Without it ReadSwitch() Poll() , ReadSwitchRaw() Those calls return Unsupported ; the display works NowMs() Poll() timestamps and idle timers, NotifyActivity() Poll() and NotifyActivity() return Unsupported Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged A port with every hook: class FullPort : public isf15acp4 :: SpiInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_gpio_write ( kVccGpio , false ) && platform_gpio_write ( kResGpio , true ) && platform_spi_init (); } bool Write ( isf15acp4 :: DataKind kind , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_gpio_write ( kDcGpio , kind == isf15acp4 :: DataKind :: Data ) && platform_spi_write ( data , len ); } bool GpioSet ( isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin pin , isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { const bool active = ( signal == isf15acp4 :: GpioSignal :: ACTIVE ); return ( pin == isf15acp4 :: CtrlPin :: Reset ) ? platform_gpio_write ( kResGpio , ! active ) : platform_gpio_write ( kVccGpio , active ); } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // Optional: the switch pin's physical level. The driver applies the polarity. bool ReadSwitch ( bool & high ) noexcept { high = platform_gpio_read ( kSwitchGpio ); return true ; } // Optional: a free-running millisecond counter; it may wrap. uint32_t NowMs () noexcept { return platform_millis (); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( isf15acp4 :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level > isf15acp4 :: LogLevel :: Warning ) { return ; } platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } private : static constexpr int kDcGpio = 3 ; static constexpr int kVccGpio = 4 ; static constexpr int kSwitchGpio = 5 ; static constexpr int kResGpio = 11 ; }; isf15acp4 :: Error RecoverFromDarkPanel ( isf15acp4 :: ISF15ACP4 < FullPort >& panel ) { // The bus is write only: a brown-out of the logic supply cannot be detected, only repaired. This // runs the power-down, the start-up and the display-on again. return panel . Reinitialize (). error ; } A GpioSet() that returns void is a compile error: the driver must see a failed pin write, because it drives the supply with it. The compile-fail tests check that rule and the signatures of every hook.

EnsureInitialized (); ! r ) { // 1. reset, configure, clear: the supply is still off return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // Bus or InvalidArgument: check wiring and Config } if ( auto r = panel . DisplayOn (); ! r ) { // 2. only now is the 15 V supply enabled and the panel on return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); } if ( auto r = panel . DrawRectangle ( 0 , 0 , 95 , 63 , isf15acp4 :: kWhite ); ! r ) { // 3. draw return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); } static_cast < void > ( panel . docs.text: Recurring defects ¶ The defects that reached an independent reviewer or the first CI run of more than one driver, one entry per class. Review skills cite these ids; the mechanization policy says where each class is caught and when it moves up a level. Append new findings to the entry they belong to, or add an entry (see the policy). Evidence names the driver, the review round ( reviews/<driver>-review<N>.md , finding id) or the CI run ( reports/<driver>-ci-*.txt ). Code examples are generic and minimal; none quotes a datasheet or a standard. Detection levels: lint (a script in the preflight or the gate, no judgement), test (a model knob, a mutation, a fuzz property or a compile-fail case that fails when the defect is present), review (a named reviewer asks one question). Status: enforced is in the template now; planned is the target, tracked in the policy's backlog, and until it lands the level below it (test, then review) is what protects the driver.
